newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Europe launches drive to curb drugs, crime.
newsitem.headline: Europe launches drive to curb drugs, crime.

text.p: European Union leaders launched a new drive on Saturday to crack down on the international menace of organised crime and drug trafficking in a bid to allay fears among the 15-state bloc's 370 million citizens.

With rising drug addiction rates and more illicit narcotics entering the Union, Ireland has given crime a high-profile during its six-month EU presidency as part of a broader move to create an "area of freedom, security and justice" in Europe.

"I believe the enhanced efforts we're making in the area of crime...bring the (EU) enterprise closer to the people," Irish Prime Minister John Bruton told a news conference at the end of the EU summit in Dublin.
Summit leaders agreed to improve cooperation, seeking to convince international drug barons that Europe would no longer tolerate major crime gangs peddling hard drugs.
Better co-ordination between member state law enforcement agencies tracking the movement of drugs within the bloc will be backed up by tougher jail terms for those caught trafficking.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl summed up the dilemma facing leaders trying to increase freedom of movement while making the bloc safer against terrorists and crime gangs.
"The public must not think: 'Now the borders are open in Europe, but we have lost our internal security' -- they must think the opposite," he told reporters.
Ireland has crusaded against the drugs threat which has exploded on the small island state in recent years, creating an estimated 10,000 heroin addicts in Dublin alone.
The anti-drug backlash was further stoked in the summer after a drug baron allegedly hired a contract killer to gun down Veronica Guerin, the nation's top investigative reporter.

Member states also pledged to curb domestic drug production, focusing on synthetic drugs, such as Ecstacy, but also outlawing the growing of cannabis under glass or polythene, except for legitimate hemp businesses.

They will improve the flow of information between forensic laboratories on the chemical profiling of seized drugs, increase joint customs surveillance operations and set up a directory of operational skills and knowledge.
As part of a broader debate on crime and security, the Hague-based Europol will be given a greater operational role.
"We're very keen to work with Europol. Many of the problems of crime that afflict northern Europe are international," British Prime Minister John Major told reporters.

The Netherlands, which takes over the EU presidency next month and has been sharply criticised for being too soft on drugs, joined the call for tougher action, but remains unwilling to abandon a 20-year experiment in tolerating the use of small amounts of soft drugs and close down its "coffee-shops".

France protests that Dutch laxity has led to thousands of young "tourists" flocking to The Netherlands to buy cheap and readily-available drugs which are then circulated in France and other neighbouring countries.
But, after "friendly and constructive" talks, both countries agreed to lift reservations on the package and talk further on how to fight drug addiction within the common crime policy.
French diplomats, insisting border checks would remain in the north to try and prevent drug "tourism", said the deal was "a first step", with more work needed on harmonising drug laws.
Dutch sources agreed the impetus had now switched from a public row between Paris and The Hague over liberal Dutch laws.
"It's moved on to a more technical level," one aide said.
"On reflection...what's been agreed...is a good step in the right direction. There is no fuel for further misunderstandings or bitterness," said another diplomat.
The EU will press other nations to join the war on crime in an attempt to stem the flood of illicit drugs into the bloc from eastern Europe, the Caribbean, central Asia and Latin America.
